segments.text: Primary and foreign keys: how Oracle defines them, and how you manage them.
A primary key identifies each row of a table. In student, that is the student id column.
It combines two rules: the value must be unique, and it can never be NULL.
A table can have many unique columns, but only one primary key. Oracle builds an index for it, to find duplicates fast.
Enrolment needs two columns to identify a row, the student and the course: a composite primary key.
Each id repeats on its own: S zero one twice, C ten three times. But each pair appears only once.
Enrol Ana in Databases again, and Oracle refuses: O R A zero zero zero zero one, unique constraint violated.
Email is UNIQUE too, but it is not the key, so it may be NULL. Eva has no email.
A second NULL email is accepted: NULL is not equal to anything, so it never counts as a duplicate.
A primary key is never NULL. Insert a student without an id, and Oracle refuses: O R A zero one four zero zero.
A foreign key links a child row to its parent. Each enrolment refers to an existing student and an existing course.
Enrol a student that does not exist, S zero nine, and the insert fails with O R A zero two two nine one: parent key not found.
The other way round, deleting course C ten, which still has enrolments, fails with O R A zero two two nine two: child record found.
What happens to the children when a parent is deleted? The foreign key decides, with its ON DELETE clause.
With ON DELETE CASCADE, the children go too. Delete Ana, and her two enrolments disappear.
ON DELETE SET NULL keeps the children, but empties their foreign key. Write nothing, and the delete is rejected while children exist.
Oracle has no ON UPDATE: primary keys should not change.
Name your constraints with the CONSTRAINT keyword. Otherwise Oracle makes up a name, like sys C and a number.
To add a constraint to a table that already exists, use ALTER TABLE, ADD CONSTRAINT. Oracle first checks that the existing rows obey it.
Here, every course id must exist in course.
The dictionary view USER CONSTRAINTS lists them. The type says what each one is: P primary key, R foreign key, U unique, and C check, which includes NOT NULL.
DISABLE CONSTRAINT switches one off, for a bulk load for example, and its status shows DISABLED.
ENABLE switches it back on, after checking every row. And DROP CONSTRAINT removes it for good.
Practise it in the SQL section of the course site.
